newsitem.title: UK: Tempers high as Church of England debates gays.
newsitem.headline: Tempers high as Church of England debates gays.

text.p: Gay Christians protested outside the Church of England's General Synod on Monday as church leaders prepared for a controversial debate about homosexual clergy.
The debate, on the fourth day of the Church's annual synod in York, northern England, has threatened to spark even more anger than the 1992 decision to ordain women priests.

It came on the day Britain's new Labour government moved towards lowering the age of consent for homosexuals from 18 to 16 by saying it would not contest a case before the European Court of Human Rights.
Hours before the debate was due to begin, a crowd of gay Christians began a vigil outside the meeting hall, singing hymns under a banner reading "We're praying for an inclusive church."

The debate is being introduced to the synod by London archdeacon David Gerrard as a private members' motion entitled "Issues in Human Sexuality" and follows a 1991 bishops' report of the same name. That report sanctioned committed homosexual relationships in the laity but not for the clergy.
A strong evangelical movement within the Church of England, which leads the worldwide Anglican community of 80 million people, considers homosexuality a sin that should never be tolerated.
This will be the first time the issue has been discussed at a synod, the church's parliament, since a debate in 1981 when it voted that "homosexual acts fall short of (God's) ideal".

The Church does not condemn homosexuality, but neither does it give it its blessing and its head, the Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey, has said the church sees only two acceptable lifestyles -- marriage or celibacy.
Reverend Richard Kirker, general secretary of the Lesbian and Gay Christian Movement (LGCM), said the debate was a step forward but accused the church of hypocrisy in dealing with gay priests.

A survey of 1,200 Church of England clergy, published on Sunday by the LGCM, showed that 37 bishops, some of whom are now dead or retired, knowingly ordained, licensed or employed gay priests, despite this being against the church's policy.

"It is clear that there is a church-within-a-church and it is obvious the church now has no option but to drop the damaging and dishonest pretence that it is not ordaining practising homosexuals in considerable numbers," Kirker said.
Kirker estimates there are around 2,000 gay clergy in Britain.
He said the debate itself was unlikely to resolve much this time because gay clergy fear if they speak out they could damage their careers in the church.
"We know of clergy who are members of the synod, who are gay and who want to speak out but have been told by the bishops that they can say goodbye to their jobs if they do so."

He said he was also disappointed the motion itself was very general and the bishops have said no further amendments will be allowed. Amendments already tabled harden the motion against the acceptance of homosexuality, he said.
